extracted.intended_audience: Researchers who submit manuscripts to Nature Cell Biology and scientists who review for the journal (authors and referees)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how manuscripts submitted to Nature Cell Biology are handled, the criteria editors use to triage/send for peer review, how reviewers are chosen and expected to behave, and the editorial decision and revision policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal scope / subject fit
rubrics_metrics.description: The purview of Nature Cell Biology includes cell biology research in the broadest sense, from fundamental processes that govern cellular homeostasis and responses to external and internal cues, to cellular behaviour in tissues during development and in disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts are assigned to the editor responsible for that particular area; that editor assesses the manuscript in detail and discusses it with the editorial team. Fit to the journal's broad cell-biology remit is a primary consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for sending a paper out for review
rubrics_metrics.description: We consider various factors when deciding whether to send a paper out for review, among which is the advance provided over the literature, whether the topic is of broad interest to cell biologists, and the level of development of the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the editors aim for consistent decisions among conceptually related areas, each paper is ultimately evaluated on its own merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting reviewers is a crucial part of an editor’s work. We aim to engage researchers who are not only experts on the topic but who are also constructive, fair and timely in their assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors choose referees for both expertise and for the quality/constructiveness of their expected assessment; reviewer timeliness is an explicit consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author referee suggestions and exclusions policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Although we welcome referee suggestions by our authors, we are not bound to follow them. However, we do honour up to three referee exclusions if authors ask us to avoid certain experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may propose referees but editors retain final choice; authors may request up to three exclusions which the journal will respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review anonymity and double-blind option
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review at Nature Cell Biology is anonymous unless a reviewer chooses to reveal their identity and, since 2015, we have offered the option of double-blind peer-review for authors who wish to remain anonymous to reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default is anonymity of reviewers; authors may opt for double-blind to conceal their identities from reviewers; reviewers may choose to sign their reports if they wish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-review editorial deliberation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the referees submit their reports, the handling editor discusses these in detail in the team, including with the chief editor, to decide whether to pursue the manuscript further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers may span areas and techniques, leading to diverse referee requests; the editorial team actively deliberates rather than relying on a simple tally of recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evaluation of referee perspectives (not vote-counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether to proceed further with a manuscript, Nature Cell Biology editors do not simply consider the number of positive versus negative referee recommendations. Rather, we critically evaluate the perspective of each referee and of the authors, focusing on the paper’s key messages and whether or how they can be strengthened, in order to reach a fair and informed decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors weigh the content and viewpoints of reports and the authors' responses; the central criterion is the paper's key messages and potential to be strengthened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial synthesis and guidance for revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When inviting a revision, apart from sending authors the full referee reports, we also provide detailed guidance regarding the necessary revisions by synthesizing the referee points that the authors should address as a priority, consolidating similar concerns raised by different reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consolidate and prioritize referee concerns for authors to address, helping focus revisions on the most important issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial circumscription and overruling of referee requests
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition we circumscribe the scope of the revisions by editorially overruling referee requests that are peripheral or too open-ended. The referees are informed of the decision and the comments of the other referees, including points on which we overruled, so that they are aware of the rationale behind our decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may overrule peripheral or overly open-ended referee requests to keep revision scope reasonable and will communicate those editorial choices to referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial engagement for clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Reaching the post-review decision is an active process during which the editor may engage in further discussions with all parties involved, for example by asking referees for clarifications or comments on issues raised by another referee, or by consulting with the authors about specific referee questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may solicit clarifications from referees or authors to resolve issues before making final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of reviewer continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreeing to review a paper for Nature Cell Biology is taken as agreeing to assess subsequent versions, as we strive to maintain consistency in the reviewing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected to review revised versions to preserve continuity across review rounds, unless otherwise agreed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent experts for disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: However, in cases of contrasting views by referees or key disagreements between authors and referees, we enlist independent experts to provide input on those specific points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors recruit independent experts to arbitrate or give additional perspective on points of major disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons for rejection after peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts may not be successful after peer-review for various reasons, including limited novelty, interest to a more specialised section of the field, questionable biological relevance, insufficient mechanistic development, or major technical or conceptual problems raised by the referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These substantive shortcomings—novelty, breadth of interest, biological relevance, mechanistic depth, and technical/conceptual soundness—are key grounds for negative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision time/cost threshold (six-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: We support the rapid dissemination of research and therefore, we would not invite a revision if addressing key issues would likely require more than six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary work to make the manuscript publishable is expected to take longer than ~6 months, the editors will generally decline rather than invite revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and disagreement handling
rubrics_metrics.description: When authors contact the journal because they disagree with a negative decision, we consider their scientific arguments, proposals for additional experiments and, if the paper was peer reviewed, their responses to the referee concerns, in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will consider appeals but are unlikely to reverse a decision unless an important aspect was missed by editors or referees, or substantial revisions have addressed previous concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript transfer and sharing peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure that publication is not unduly delayed we also consider whether a manuscript we decline would be suitable for another journal in the Nature family and whether it might be in the authors’ interests to transfer the paper to that journal using our automated manuscript transfer system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers can save authors time by avoiding reformatting; for peer-reviewed manuscripts, referee reports and identities are also transferred (with permission), enabling the receiving journal to make decisions based on existing reviews. Editors may consult sister journals about suitability and expected revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial mission and commitment to constructive, timely process
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature Cell Biology aims to publish the most striking and high quality cell biology research while offering a constructive and timely editorial process and peer-review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal engages closely with authors and referees and welcomes suggestions to improve aspects of the process (contact: cellbio@nature.com).
